utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Mr. Gajic, I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everybody. Your Honour, the Defence has a request. Yesterday with the witness Acimovic, we used two documents, 65 ter 2063, and 65 ter 2064. Those documents have been used in the previous proceedings and they were part of the package according to 92 ter submitted by the Prosecution. Those documents were used yesterday in the courtroom with the witness, and we would like to tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I don't have the documents with me. We will come back to that later. I think that was an omission due to the -- the end of the hearing of yesterday. At this point in time, I would like to deal with another matter related to exhibits, in relation to the witness we are hearing today. The Chamber is seized of the Prosecution's supplemental motion for leave to amend its 65 ter exhibit list with two additional exhibits filed on the 3rd of February. By its motion, the Prosecution requests leave to supplement its Rule 65 ter exhibit list to add two demographic reports prepared by Witness Dr. Helge Brunborg in April 2009. On Monday, Mr. Gajic, on behalf of Mr. Tolimir, orally responded to this motion. Mr. Gajic submits that the motion should be denied because the Prosecution's request is already contained in Prosecution confidential notice filed on 26th November 2009 and the motion is, thus, moot. Further, he argues that he is awaiting a decision on the said notice and the accused's notice filed on 14th of January 2010. Finally, he states that the accused does not accept Dr. Brunborg's reports and he wishes to cross-examine him. Following this oral response, the Prosecution replied, Mr. McCloskey argues that the accused has been on notice of Dr. Brunborg's two reports for a long time. The Chamber first notes that according to the 26th of November, 2009, Prosecution supplemental notice, the two reports of Dr. Brunborg are updates of his reports created for the Karadzic case on the 9th of April, 2009, after the filing of the Prosecution's notice -- first notice filed on the 13th of March, 2009. The Trial Chamber is of the view that these reports which are updated versions of his prior reports are prima facie relevant to this case and of probative value. Further, by decision of the Chamber on 3rd of November, 2009, the transcript of Dr. Brunborg's testimony and his associated exhibit were provisionally admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter which guarantees the accused the right of cross-examining Dr. Brunborg. That is why Mr. Brunborg is scheduled to testify today pursuant to Rule 92 ter. While the two reports are quite voluminous, the first report is 105 pages long and the second report is 239 pages long, since the filing of the aforementioned notice, the accused has been notified of their intended use with Dr. Brunborg even though they have not been added to the 65 ter exhibit list until now. In this respect, the Chamber emphasises that the primary purpose of the 65 ter exhibit list is to give notice to the accused and his Defence team so that he can prepare his Defence and that by simply disclosing the material to the accused and his Defence team, the Prosecution does not fulfil its obligation under Rule 65 ter (E)(iii). Yet, in the specific circumstances of this case, the Chamber considers that the Prosecution showed good cause for seeking the addition of the reports and that the accused is not unduly burdened by the addition at this stage of the proceedings. For these reasons, the Chamber finds that it is in the interests of justice to grant the addition of the two reports to the 65 ter exhibit list. The motion is thereby granted. If there are no matters to raise, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please take the earphones. Welcome to the Tribunal again. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. Mr. McCloskey has questions for you during his examination-in-chief. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Brunborg. Can you start off by just telling us your full name.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Helge, H-e-l-g-e.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your last name?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Brunborg, spelled B-r-u-n-b-o-r-g.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And as we'll soon go through a summary, you've testified many times here at the OTP as a demographic expert for the Prosecution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for this particular case have you had a chance to review your testimony in the Popovic et al case?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I've looked at it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And but for perhaps some updated data and information, would your answers basically be the same, if you were asked the same questions again?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. President, at this time I have a series of documents from the prior testimony to offer. I have spoken briefly to the Court Officer and it would -- it would begin with 65 ter 06660, which is the transcript of Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We'll deal with that first and admit it into evidence. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit numbers will be assigned and a memo will be circulated at a later stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But the Popovic transcript should have an exhibit number now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P1774. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, we have a total of 29 such exhibits that will be handled as the Court Officer just stated. The 2009 reports that were just the subject of your ruling, I will -- I will get to and ask briefly about the witness and so we'll get the numbers when they come up if -- if you would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I have a -- for this witness a relatively short summary, Mr. President, and the testimony will be a bit longer than perhaps some of the 92 ter testimonies just because of the subject matter, and because the discussions with Mr. Gajic, the great interest the Defence has. I think it's a good idea to hear from the witness. And I encourage you to interrupt me at any time with questions on this material, and so that it is as clear as possible. I'll try to hit the high points, but I'm sure I won't hit everything and that you may be interested in. And I hope not to take two hours. Dr. Brunborg and I have done this before and we should be able to be much lower than that, I hope. But we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. It is appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so the summary is: Dr. Brunborg is an economist and demographer by profession and is employed as a senior researcher in the statistics department of the Norwegian national institute statistics, known as Statistics Norway. He has primarily worked on projects for Statistics Norway but has also worked on demographics projects in Palestine, Mozambique, Botswana, Bangladesh, Albania, and in Afghanistan for the United Nations Fund for Population Activities as well as other international projects. From June 1997 through the end of 1998, Dr. Brunborg worked for the Office of the Prosecutor for the ICTY. He was first tasked with collecting and evaluating data on population changes in Bosnia and Herzegovina from the war period, 1992 through 1995. In late 1998 or early 1999, Dr. Brunborg was asked by the Office of the Prosecutor to compile a list of missing persons related to the events in Srebrenica in July of 1995. Dr. Brunborg has testified regarding his work for the OTP in ICTY trials of Krstic, Blagojevic, Milosevic, Perisic, Milutinovic, Popovic, and Djordjevic. His first Srebrenica missing report was completed in 2000, and he updated that report in 2005 and worked with OTP demographer Ewa Tabeau in the latest report finalised in 2009, which will be the subject of some additional questions. To form the list of Srebrenica missing persons, Dr. Brunborg relied on his analysis of the list of missing persons from Bosnia and Herzegovina generated by the International Committee of the Red Cross, and the list of missing persons compiled by the NGO, Physicians for Human Rights. Dr. Brunborg extracted from those two lists those individuals whose disappearance was related to the fall of Srebrenica. That is, those individuals who were reported missing by family members on or after 11 July 1995 from locations around Srebrenica. He received those directions from the Srebrenica OTP team. In his analysis to determine the accuracy of the ICRC and PHR missing lists, Dr. Brunborg used various data sources, including the 1991 census conducted in the former Yugoslavia, a voters' registration list collected by the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe in 1997 and on later dates. In addition, he used the BiH army records of fallen soldiers, ICMP DNA identification records for Srebrenica-related victims and other records, as noted in his reports. As part of his work, Dr. Brunborg reviewed and analysed claims made by various groups. It claimed that the number of missing from Srebrenica was exaggerated in the ICRC list, some of those claims included the following: Large numbers of persons on the missing list were, in fact, alive and were on the voters' registration list of 1996; number 2, large numbers of persons on the missing list had died before the fall of Srebrenica and were thus not related to the fall of Srebrenica; 3, large numbers of BiH soldiers from Srebrenica went missing or died before the fall of Srebrenica and were thus not related to the fall of Srebrenica. Dr. Brunborg did not find any substance to any of the above claims or any other such claim. Dr. Brunborg found no indication of any missing reports of fictitious persons on the part of Muslims who reported their relatives missing to ICRC and PHR. In his 12 February 2000 report, his first report, Dr. Brunborg concluded that at least 7.475 persons were missing or dead from Srebrenica, and in his most recent report of 9 April 2009, Dr. Brunborg has concluded that at least 7.905 people were missing or dead. Dr. Brunborg testified in Popovic that the process of determining the total number of persons who were missing or dead after the fall of Srebrenica is an ongoing process and that new data, exhumations and identification would likely increase the number of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And, Dr. Brunborg, you have gone over your experience and the -- defined your field in your previous testimony so I won't ask you to get into that. But one thing you do state is that your work in the Tribunal led you to develop a new area of -- in the field of demography called the demography of conflicts. And can you briefly tell us what this demography of conflicts is and how it is related to your previous work in statistics and demography work.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Thank you. First, I wouldn't take responsibility for developing that area myself. There are many people who have worked in the field. But it came -- became clear that in conflict areas the problems regarding data and methods are special and unique and often very difficult, and that there was a need to place special attention on these issues. So that's why we -- we organised a seminar on conflict demography in 2003 which resulted in two special issues of well-known journals and "Journal of Peace Research" and the "European Journal of Population" and a book on conflict demography edited by me and my co-author here, Ewa Tabeau, and previous co-worker, Henrik Urdal. In this way, I have been chairing a working group or a panel of the International Union for the Scientific Study of Population on these issues. At conferences -- there have been special demography conferences. There have been several sessions on the demography of conflict which has received many contributions. As you know, there are many conflicts in the world and there is often a need to estimate the fatalities, infant mortality in conflict areas, refugees, even how fertility births, and migrations and marriages are affected by conflicts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you for a clarification. You mentioned two people with whom you edited this journal. One was Ewa Tabeau and the other name is missing on the record, and, therefore, I would like to ask you to repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. The other name was Henrik Urdal, who worked with me here in 1999 and co-authored the report mentioned by Mr. McCloskey which was published -- not published but was finished in 2000 and used in the Krstic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now as we know, the task that you were asked to perform was to look at the ICRC lists, the PHR lists and evaluate them to create a credible missing list of people that went missing in Srebrenica. And, again briefly, what was it about your profession as a demographer that qualified you to be able to review and analyse critically the ICRC missing list? Just the high points so the Court understands why you were called on for this task and why you may be qualified to take it on.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Thank you. I think there were two reasons: First, my general education and training and experience in demography. It is important to understand and have knowledge about demographic processes or which death is an important and a final process, of course. And, second, my experience in Norway and many other countries working with data on individuals. Especially in Norway we do a lot of demographic work based on registers, administrative registers, and we match data on individuals from different sources to come up with the research and analysis. For example, we may match records on deaths by -- with other records on education to study how education is related to mortality or the other way around, actually. And so I thought it was useful to have this experience on working with data on individuals to work here, and that was the approach taken right from the beginning, that it's important to collect and analysis data on individuals because it is, in a way, more difficult to lie with data on individuals. During the war, the conflicts in Bosnia, there were many numbers floating around on the number of deaths. When I arrived, there were numbers ranging from as low as 20.000 deaths for all of Bosnia for all ethnicities, of course. Two more than 300.000. And they could not all be true, and many of these have been collected by adding press reports and other reports, number of victims and such and such an incident added together and methods of prorating and other methods to estimate deaths in areas where they did not have any data, which I did not have any data for. And so they were added together, and, as I said, widely different estimates, that is one of the reasons why the Tribunal wanted somebody with experience in population statistics and demographic to look at the data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And as came out, I think, in the last trial your -- most of your experience was from -- working for Statistics Norway on Norwegian material and I think you've testified that in Norway each person in the census has a number and things are fairly well organised, the population is relatively small and it's a much, much different world than the former Yugoslavia. Were you able to take your experience from that Norwegian society and adapt it to what you had described coming out of the war with different numbers and press reports?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Definitely. First, I would say that I also have experience in countries with efficient data, like Botswana and the census there. But there are many similarities between Norway and Bosnia. The population is about the same, between 4 and 5 -- population size, between 4 and 5 million. Botswana, as the rest of the former Yugoslavia, has regular censuses of reasonably good quality. They even have a personal identification number introduced in the former Yugoslavia in 1981. And which would be then a good basis for linking records from different sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We'll get into that a little bit -- a little bit later. Let me just jump right into it. When you were tasked with creating this Srebrenica list, who gave you the, basically, guide-line that it should be people gone missing from 11 July and beyond, in certain areas around Srebrenica? Where -- who gave you that guide-line in your tasking?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That was investigators at OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And was that part of the team that I was a legal officer on?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And first, can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what this ICRC list is and how it was created, just briefly so they understand what it is that you're going to be evaluating.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: ICRC is the a humanitarian organisation based in Switzerland, International Committee of the Red Cross, and they collect such lists to -- in conflict situations basically to make it possible to people to find each other. Again, when in a war -- in a conflict, and many families are split, and it's difficult to know where people are. Some are arrested, some are dead, some are just fleeing to another part of the country or to another country altogether. And before Internet and cell phones it was very difficult to locate people, so that is one major reason why the ICRC started to collect data on -- in all over the former Yugoslavia, and especially in Bosnia, and especially on Srebrenica after the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you roughly know how long ICRC has been taking -- doing this kind of work in conflict situations?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't know. But Henry Dunant established the ICRC, I think, more than 100 years ago. And when they started establishing such lists, I don't know. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you describe the list itself and how it was created by -- how they actually did it.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At this point in time, you should drink some water, it helps. And I would like to draw your attention on the reporter's, court reporter's note, it is -- you are using the same language and therefore you should pause between question and answer. Otherwise, it is very difficult for the report and especially for the interpreters who have to interpreter all what you are saying into different languages. Now you may answer the question, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And may you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Can you just basically tell us how this list was put together.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Soon after the fall of Srebrenica, the ICRC started -- they established some kind of office in Tuzla and relatives could come to them and register family members that were lost, they were missing, that they hadn't seen since the fall of Srebrenica. And they continued in Tuzla and Sarajevo and other parts of Bosnia for several years. In fact, they still continue to collect data on missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is their report -- was it published publicly?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. Several lists have been published. First on paper in those days. There was no Internet. And thick books with names of more than 7.000, or, for all of Bosnia, many more people missing in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was the basic information they took besides obviously the name of the missing relative? What else did they get -- did they try to get from the relative?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I'm taking a break as requested by the Judge. First name and last name, of course, of the missing family member, then father's name. The dates they last saw the person alive or the -- they heard that -- or the date the person died if they knew that. The place where they believe that the person went missing or the last place seen missing. And place of birth. And place of residence. Was the basic -- and gender also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what problems you came across in the accuracy of some of that data as you were studying it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The first thing - excuse me - the first thing we did was to look for duplicates to see if somebody has been wrongly registered twice or more. And we did find some duplicates. In a chaotic situation it is no surprise that often, say, two different family members come forward and register the same person twice, sometimes with slightly different information. One may remember the date of birth more accurately than the other person. So it is difficult to find these duplicates. But we managed to find them using various methods. That was a problem. And date of birth was not always complete or accurate because, again, in a chaotic situation, people did not always remember their family member's exact date of birth. Usually they remember the year of birth, it is it missing for very few people but the exact date is not always known. Those were the major problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. In the summary I mentioned, another list that you had said you used, the Physicians for Human Rights, or the PHR list, can you briefly describe -- the Court has heard about PHR as an NGO that supplied pathologists for the exhumations, but can you tell what did PHR do in this context, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: You may have been told that their goal was quite different. Their goal was to help families identify lost and killed family members. So they created a so-called antemortem database. And they collected -- they started collecting the data on Srebrenica in 1996 and collecting more detailed information on, say, physical appearance of the persons missing, especially clothing, special other characteristics about teeth and other issues to help in the identification of exhumed bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt for a moment. Do you have any problem with the seat, with the chair you are sitting on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Does it look like?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it looks like. That you are struggling with the chair. Perhaps the Court Usher can assist you with fixing some parts of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is leaning backwards too much, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the problem I realise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for -- I sort of become more relaxed and ... Okay. That is better. Thank you, Your Honour, for making my position better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So how long was PHR seeing relatives and taking this information you've just described?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: For a couple of years, I believe. I think they finished their work in 1998 or 1999. The reason could possibly be funding problems. But their database still exists and the data are used by other organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you get full computerised access to that data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you get eventually access in a computerised electronic format of the ICRC missing lists and its various updates?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did the PHR data have similar problems that you just described for the ICRC data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes and no. The -- there were not as many duplicates, as far as I remember. I don't know if there were any, but we checked. The data -- the date of birth was complete in more cases and perhaps even correct in more cases because the data were collected in more -- in a more calm situation when not right after women had fled from Srebrenica. So people came forward and perhaps they had some documents to show the -- the exact date of birth and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So for your initial work, what did you do with these two reports to make a one -- one list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, first, we had several versions of the ICRC missing lists, so we had to merge those. They were -- they were mostly overlapping but they were from different years and so there were some additional names. So we merged -- actually, merged all the lists. We had two lists from the ICRC and two from PHR. So we merged all these lists, removing all overlap and comparing information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you make an effort, as you have previously described, to get rid of any duplicates from PHR and ICRC?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, we did. But it was not always straightforward to know which of the duplicates, pair of duplicate records, we should delete because sometimes the information was different, and we -- we had to give some attention to that also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was the -- was there another data source that helped you solve that problem or determine whether these people on the list were actually real people?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. Fortunately for us there was a census in 1991, 31st of March, right before the war broke out in all of Yugoslavia and in Bosnia. And we got hold of a -- an electronic data base, data files for that census with the name, date of birth, et cetera, for everybody in -- who lived in the country in -- on the 31st of March, 1991. The census was taken in more quiet circumstances and we believe that the -- many of the data items were a better quality in the census including the date of birth. Moreover, it was complete, so if there were -- say we were worried about duplicates whether two records that were almost the same, whether they represented one person or two different persons, we could check in the census to see whether there were two persons with almost the same information. Say, same name, same father's name but slightly different dates of birth. But there were also problems with the census. The most serious problem was that the names were often misspelled. The reason for that is that scanning was used. There were the -- enumerators used forms and wrote down the names of all the household members, afterwards the names were scanned but not corrected, and scanners did not always read all handwriting, so some -- there were many errors. But when we looked up visually, we could check the errors but doing -- and related develop methods to correct and improve the -- the names, the spelling of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give the Court an idea, I think you testified about it before, that no census is perfect. Can you give us an idea of roughly how accurate you think the census of the former Yugoslavia was for the millions of households that would have had to -- or millions of people that it would have had to try to account for -- just roughly, to get an idea of -- for us.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I could not give you a number on the accuracy. There's often in censuses, there's something called a post-enumeration survey where they go back to a sample of households and interview again and then compare the first census to check the records, but this was not done in Bosnia, perhaps partly because of the conflict that started in 1991. And -- but generally I would say the quality is good. Some of the problems are that -- what about people who are absent? Some people were living abroad and were included. It depends whether the census is based -- taken on the de facto or de jure basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe -- I believe your early work in 2000, you have testified you did not use the census for all the people on the list. But as your work continued, you used the census more and more. Can you describe that? So by the time we get to 2009, how were you using the census to -- to double-check the -- your list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: As I said, because of all the spelling mistakes, due to the scanning of the census forms, we could not do an automatic computer-used matching or the list of missing persons with the census in 2000. But we developed methods to correct the spelling. And one was that in a households -- in one household, different persons usually have the same surname, and if they were spelled differently, and we knew that one or two of them was a correct name, we changed -- we corrected the other names. Say, if Ljubic is a common name and Lj was often misinterpreted as a Q, so then we change Q to Lj, and there were many similar. Music was sometimes spelled with a V, Mvsic, so then we changed the V to a U. And then we get a much higher correspondence between the names in the census and the missing list, and we could do an automatic matching and find out much more, instead of checking just individuals as we had done in 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you get another major data source from a group by the name of ICMP that assisted your work?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, gradually. But I would also like to mention that -- another group that is, the -- that -- we got data from and that is the OSCE, Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe, which provided us with a list of registered voters in 1997 and 1998. Also by name even identification number. And the reason for being interested in that is that we wanted to see if some of the missing persons were -- survived the war and were wrongly registered missing, and if they registered to vote they were -- they were obviously not dead. So we did compare the missing list with the voters' list. But you asked about the ICMP, International Commission for Missing Persons, and they started their work for doing exhumations or doing DNA analysis of exhumed bodies and comparing the DNA profiles with blood samples of family members of missing members -- missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I would to put a question to clarify one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How were the list of the voters for this -- yeah, for the voters in 1997 and 1998 compiled? What was, for the national authorities, the source on which they really could rely? Did they count the people and then register, or just did they take over the information from previous lists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People had to come forward and register to vote. But they had to be enumerated in 1991, so all the registration places had -- had the census of 1991 and then people could prove their identity and say, I'm such and such a person. And if they were then found on the 1991 census list, okay, then they were ticked off as a registered voter. Those who were not enumerated in 1991, they had to prove their identity and that they lived in Bosnia and had the right to vote. So people had to come forward to register.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They had to show up personally and this is a clear indication that they really were alive at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If they were missing persons who did that. But, of course, it could be that some people, to gain political influence, used a missing person's identity or for other reasons. It could also be that when somebody showed up to register that the person doing the registration ticked off the wrong person. But we -- we can go into the -- later into the results of that comparison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When the person would come in to register, were they registering, do you recall, with the OSCE official or with a government official?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what they did. I think obviously they were Bosnians doing the registration, but whether they were official OSCE was running these registration stations or not, I'm not quite sure. I think OSCE oversaw the whole thing so I think they were in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And so you had the compiled lists that you worked on from PHR and ICRC of people that had gone missing 11 July and onward. Then you took these voters' list to compare to your lists to determine what, again, so it is perfectly clear?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, we matched then the missing persons with the voters' list to see if there were any survivors. We did find nine persons in 2000 who were on both lists. So either they were not missing, they were not dead, at least. Or there was some kind of voter registration. So to be on the safe side, we deleted those nine records from the missing lists. Later it has been shown that one of them a has been found -- identified as dead through DNA analysis and the remaining eight on that list, we don't know. It's an unresolved issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But because it was unresolved, did you -- you took those people off your lists so they're not reflected in the final number; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. And in later analysis with comparing missing with displaced person, et cetera, more people were found. I think up to 26 possible matches. And all those where there was a slight suspicious that these were survivors who were living, we took them off the lists. But we were careful to check that these were really true matches and we did not confuse person with almost the same characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Especially given the allegation they were people alive and voting on your list, I would like you to be able to explain that match process in a little more detail like you have before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So could we go to 00543, 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At this point in time, I would like to put on the record a correction. The transcript of the Popovic case was assigned today on page 5, lines 5 and 6, with the wrong exhibit number. The right number should be P1774, instead of 177 -- sorry, I misspoke again. Should be 1775, instead of 1774. I think now it's correct on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please enlarge the version I see on the screen or do I do it or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, it will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. If you need --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want me to go through that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let me, first of all, ask you is this basically something out of your report on from your testimony last time?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It's out of the 2005 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We see this as an example of a false match and so can you explain it and -- if we can blow up the English, it -- I think it's such a basic document that I -- I trust the --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir if this is sufficient or do you need the B/C/S version at the same time on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to greet everybody who is present here in the courtroom and I hope that this trial will end in accordance with God's will and not my will. Now, one thing, if we are talking generally here we should then check the pairs to see if there are some differences with the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think to deal with that the best way is that you will receive a hard copy of the B/C/S version and then you can compare. Otherwise, it is really very small and illegible. The Court Officer will provide you with a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think as we can see it is mostly Bosnian names and it's self-explanatory data, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir is receiving a hard copy of the B/C/S version now. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Dr. Brunborg, could you explain this a bit. We see the -- we have a Delic from the ICRC list and from the voters' register list of 1997, and then we have two people with the same name from the census. Tell us about why this is a false match and how you figured that out?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, at the first glance this looks -- the Abdulah Delic on the ICRC missing list, born in 1995, there is also Abdulah Delic, born in 1995, on the voters' register. So at the first glance, this looks like it's the same person. But then we notice that the father's name, Husein, is not given in the voters' register and we looked up the census and we found that, indeed, there were two Abdulah Delic born in 1995 who were enumerated in 1991. And there's the first Abdulah Delic has a father called Husein, the other person's father was Kemal. And they also had different identity numbers -- identification numbers, 183920 and 183954 for the other one. So we concluded that they represent different persons and that Abdulah Delic, whose father is Husein, is not on the list of -- on the voters' list and cannot be suspected of, if you like, being alive in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is it fair, then, to say that you kept Abdulah Delic on your list and counted him as a missing person?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another part of your report, 00542, which you've used as an example of a true match. And while we're waiting for that to come up, you mentioned, I think, there is a -- a special number that people were assigned during the census. Do you remember what that was called in Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: "Maticni broj" and it's a unique identification number. It was assigned to everybody in 1981 and people were then asked to record their identification number, their "maticni broj," when the enumerators came around to collect -- to enumerate people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the ICRC list get this number?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. They did not. But the voters' list did get their number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about PHR?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. And people would usually not know their name -- their number of relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So, again, we now see here that there is a Gabeljic, Avdo. Can you explain how you evaluated this?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, first we see there were there was one Mensur Gabeljic on the ICRC lists and after correcting a typo or a scanning mistake you see the LJ become a Q. There is also Mensur Gabeljic on the voters' register in 1997. The father's name of Avdo is given on the ICRC list but it is not given on the voters' register. Moreover, they are recorded as being born in two different years, 1970 and 1971. And so there are some differences but there are also some similarities. We checked the census and we found only one Mensur Gabeljic, born on the 28th of 11th, 1971, his father's name was registered as Avoo, but I guess it should be Avdo. But we concluded that this is a true match and that they are, indeed, representing the same person and that this Mensur Gabeljic was then excluded from our list of missing persons. It remained on the ICRC's own list, I believe, but on the OTP list it was removed, excluded, but it could be considered later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. But, in any event, the -- you may have already said this, but roughly, did you find very many people that you were able to match from the various voters' register lists and your missing list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: In 2000, we found nine, and we later we found, I think, altogether 26 in different lists. It's -- there's a table for that in the 2009 report. Some of these potential survivors have later been found to be dead. So we believe that there seems to be some -- have been some faulty registration, not necessarily for bad reasons, but just perhaps of mistakes. But we have not really found any -- many examples of real survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And going back to your list, and you testified before that you didn't find any examples of Muslim families providing fictitious missing persons. How did you look for that and is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct. We did, as I said, compare the missing list with -- with the census and we found for -- for the Srebrenica missing, we found that 87 -- we found 87 per cent of them in the 1991 census. The exact same individuals were enumerated in 1997, and for the remaining 13 per cent there could be various reasons why we did not find them. Some of them may not have been in Srebrenica in 1991 or in Bosnia. They could have been living elsewhere, say, in Serbia. And also because of -- all these spelling mistakes and all that, or lack of information, it could be -- it was difficult -- they were difficult to match or inconclusive matches. But 87 per cent is a high proportion anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, for your 2000 report where you assembled the list and you did the quality control of the voters' list, did you have -- what kind of confirmed deaths did you have to compare to your actual list, if any? For that first report, way back when.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: In 2000, there were only 70 confirmed deaths. Sixty-six of these were found on our list of missing persons then marked as dead. Two additional persons were -- have been found in Srebrenica-related graves and then were then added to the list of missing and dead. And two were -- had dates or place of disappearance that were not consistent with our rules for selecting Srebrenica-related missing, were not considered. So, to conclude, out of the almost 7.500 missing persons in the first list, 66 were found to be dead. That is, less than 1 per cent, .9 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now you've mentioned briefly ICMP and the Trial Chamber has heard through the investigators about ICMP and about how they took family reports of missing and took their blood to compare to the DNA and the bones from the graves. So they -- they've heard that. Were you able to -- in your ongoing work, after your initial work, able to get those records of DNA identified dead from Srebrenica-related graves and use that for your work?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. We started receiving reports from the ICMP on exhumed bodies whose DNA profiles had been matched to satisfaction with blood samples from family members, and we got more and more. Today we have received more than 5.000 such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, tell us. We have forensic blood identification, which I would -- might call some hard science, plus we have your demographic reports of traumatised family members, in some cases, reporting missing people which forms the guts of your list. How does this forensic identification help you or assist you in determining the validity of your work, if at all?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: First, the forensic work proves that people are really dead. They're not missing anymore. They are found dead and most of them in mass graves. Secondly, the -- this is based on a comparison of -- with blood samples drawn from family members and they came forward, family members came forward voluntarily sometime after the events in Srebrenica in -- also in less chaotic circumstances, and several, often several family members for each missing person. So their lists -- so ICMP has also a list of missing persons which we have not seen, actually. What they give us is their confirmed and what we call identified deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you compare the names of the ICMP identified deaths with the names on your missing list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, we did. That is exactly what we did. And almost all of them were found on our lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And perhaps to -- go ahead if you want to explain it more.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It would be useful if you could show the exhibits with the shaded -- based on the table in the report first, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to 65 ter 07174.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And again, perhaps -- and I will try in the future to have these for the General, but we may need a hard copy of the B/C/S, if you have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The accused will be provided with a hard copy. There is no B/C/S version I am told.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll just carefully go through this. And it is a very simple chart so it can be translated, and I will do that now for the General. It is entitled: "Overview of the progress in the DNA identification of Srebrenica missing." And then when we get down to the tables, we see the strongly outlined one is the first one, and that is the date of the OTP report, so we see the year and date. And the next one over is: Srebrenica missing by the OTP; Srebrenica identified by the ICMP; the accepted overlap is the next chart; the excluded overlap is the next chart; the next one is new victims identified; the next one is excluded potential survivors; the next one is accepted victim integrated; the next one is per cent identified; and the next one is per cent identified, number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So Dr. Brunborg what -- can you explain we see that the numbers are charging from the various reports. How does this assist you in answering my last question?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: First, this is table 12 from the -- our most recent report. And first you see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could you switch off your microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, you see that the number of missing on the OTP list has grown from 7.475 to 7.692 by a little more than 200. More interesting is perhaps that the number of identified dead has grown from 68 in 2000 to 5.555 in 2009, according to DNA analysis. We also see, if we then notice new victims. That is one -- column number 6 or so, that there were in the most recent report from ICMP there were 213 persons who were not on our list of missing persons, so we add those. We exclude 12 potential survivors, so the number of potential survivors had grown from 9 to 12. And we end up with 7.905 missing or dead persons related to the fall of Srebrenica, which has grown from almost 7.500 in 2000. So that is by little more than 400. So it is now almost 8.000, the total number. And may I finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The last column which shows the proportion identified as dead. It was .9 per cent in 2000 and it is now 66.7 per cent, which is exactly two-thirds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What does it mean "now"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Now" means November 2008. This report was finished in April 2009, based on -- the most recent ICMP report then was dated November 2008. Since then, there are -- several more reports have been received with several hundred more identified persons. But we have not had been able to analyse all that. So new data keep coming all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So how can you explain this -- I don't know -- I think over 400 new people or new numbers on your missing -- missing/dead list from the early report, 7.475, to the latest here 7-9. We know that PHR missing list was stopped after two years; the ICRC, you've explained, had 200 more people on it. But where are the other 200-plus coming from, besides the -- the updated ICRC list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: First, in what is listed as "Srebrenica missing OTP," you see that from 2008 to 2009, or, actually, from 2005 to 2009, the list grew by 29. That is additional missing persons reported by the ICRC. Then -- but -- as you indicated, the largest increase is in the number of new victims, and these are then persons who have been exhumed from graves with -- which are mass graves which are Srebrenica-related, and then -- and these are then added to the total number. And the reason is that not all families reported, we think -- is that not all families reported their missing persons as missing for various reasons. It could that be that the whole family was -- was eradicated, or there were special reasons why they did not report, living abroad, more difficult to report, say, wanting to forget the whole thing, not seeing the -- the sense or the meaning of -- of reporting, so there are various reasons. So that's why bodies are found who were not reported -- whose families did not report to ICRC. But there are also bodies -- have found that are not reported to anybody, not even ICMP, and they are not listed here but they were -- they are so-called no-name bodies and they were -- I think, the most recent report there were 294 bodies that had unique DNA profiles but could not be linked to anybody and they, of course, are not included here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I go back to line 19 of page 30, you are recorded having said: "You see that from 2008 to 2009, or, actually, from 2005 to 2009, the list grew by 29."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mh-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I know [indiscernible] but it should be 31, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, you are -- that's right. There's a difference in one because one was excluded, and why, for technical reasons. So -- and one came in addition, so it must be 31. Yeah, excuse me, I have been used to these 29 numbers -- number. I will look at it in the break to see if I can explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now from what I gather, you're saying there are several people on your final figure of 7.905 identified names that are not on your missing list. So how do you associate those people with Srebrenica, if they were not reported missing from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: First, they were reported to ICMP as associated with the fall of Srebrenica. That is the most important reason. Second, we checked the dates of disappearance or last seen alive, and the place of disappearance, and they were consistent with our criteria. And, finally, they were found in graves together with other Srebrenica-related victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So how -- you said you don't have the ICMP missing list, so how is it that you know they were reported missing to ICMP?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Because ICMP had collected blood samples from family members of missing persons, and they had their criteria for -- for inviting people to give blood samples. So this was defined by ICMP, whether this was a Srebrenica-related missing person or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me put up another chart that you had just recently, in the last day or two days, asked us to help your testimony, which is the reason we didn't have the translation for the other one, Mr. President. We just got this specific request. But it is 07173.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, to be clear, both these last two charts came out of his report and should be translated, and I have those numbers on e-court, if it's necessary. But this particular chart, I -- really doesn't need translation, I don't think, as soon as I read the top of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I add that it is Figure 5 in the report. On page 19 in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's B/C/S 22 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this says at the top: "Age distribution of Srebrenica-related missing and dead persons, all missing versus confirmed dead (in per cent)." And which one of these particular charts did you want to discuss?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I have split up the figure in the report in the two parts. The first -- the top panel shows the age distribution of persons on our missing lists. These are -- has nothing to do with being confirmed dead or not. So it is just the pure age distribution based on information on missing persons. That is the top one. The next panel with dark bars shows the age distribution of those who have been identified as dead, and if can you see both the top ones at the same time, you will notice there is some similarity. There is, for instance, a bump at age 55 to 59. It is higher than the preceding and the following age groups. And also for 25 to 29, the number is lower than for the preceding. So when we put these together, these two sets of bars, remember, these are relative numbers, percentages so they add up to 100 percent. At the bottom, the bottom panel, there have been put together as in the report, Figure 5. And you see the striking similarity. You again see that the 55 to 59 group is -- has higher -- has a higher percentage than the preceding and following age groups, which there may be good reasons for. We did this similar graphs both in year 2000 and 2005 reports and the age distributions are becoming more and more similar which shows that they come from the same population. You could say this is a population of missing persons, and in exhumation there's a random process or the -- the exhumed persons come from the same population. If that come from a different population, the age distributions would most likely have looked quite different. So even the special characteristics of these humps and bumps in the age distribution of the missing appears in the age distribution or those confirmed dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that you would get a -- a pretty good age from a person confirmed dead, as the family member would be able to give you a good age for their missing relative; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. Before the DNA analysis started, then -- and before bodies were identified, the age was determined by physical anthropologists, and they could only estimate the age in very wide age groups and with considerable uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you have testified in several trials and as the record reflects, there are have been expert -- there has been at least one expert from the Defence, I think Ms. --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Radovanovic, thank you. And your data has been challenged in -- in some of the trials and criticised. Did you find any -- any justified criticisms or inaccuracies in your work that was pointed out by the Defence experts over the years?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Mrs. Radovanovic, herself, a demographer, was given access to the date in a room here at the Tribunal. She was not allowed to take any data out of the Tribunal, but she analysed the data and she found ten or so duplicates on our missing lists indicating that we were -- well, she didn't use the word cheating but some strong words about our methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for one second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we please have a reference so that we would know what this is about, so that we would have arguments and see whether the Defence can use them rather than have the witness verify what he wrote and deny what others said about the same subject. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Her testimony is part of the record and it's -- it's in the record of his testimony. It's -- her reports are -- are part of the record that have been provided to the Defence. And I'm just asking him to briefly outline the small areas where she was correct and have him explain it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may add that this was in the trial against Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh. Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That helps. We need our first break now, but before we do that, I would like to ask both parties to liaise on the matter. Is there translation necessary for 65 ter 7173 and 65 ter 07174 we just used and have it on the screen. But there's no translation yet, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 7173 can be found on -- in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct. I was told by the Registry there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, for both of those, there are. It would be 32 for 7174. We're having a slight bit of confusion. But there's translations in the report and we'll make sure that that's on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I think we need a clarification in relation to all the other exhibits you have tendered which were used during the previous trial. Do they all have a translation into B/C/S and, if not, we would like to know which of them don't have a translation. But you -- I would like to receive your answer after the break. We have to adjourn for half an hour, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we continue, just briefly, Mr. Gajic, on behalf of the Defence, tendered two exhibits used with the last witness of yesterday. These are 65 ter 02064 and 02063, two OTP interviews with the witness of yesterday. They will be received as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this two documents will be assigned the following exhibit numbers: 65 ter document 0264 shall be assigned D157. And the second document 65 ter 0263 shall be assigned D158.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The number is not correctly recorded, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first one should be 157, D157, Defence document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's correct. Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and, Mr. President, the witness had a brief comment to the Court Officer about something that he would like to clarify, so I would -- and we all know that. So if can he can ask the witness to clarify the issue he wanted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You pointed out my fault, the arithmetic. So thank you for that. In Table 12 which was one of the exhibits, the reason is that the number on the 2009 OTP list was revised from 7661 to 7663 in -- after that list was produced because of duplicates that were not really duplicates and one survivor and one who was not a survivor and was found dead. This is all explained on page 6, the second paragraph from the bottom. But I have become used to thinking of the difference between those two lists of 2005 and 2009 as being 29. But it should, of course, be 31. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I was asking you whether the Defence expert that -- Ms. Radovanovic, that testified in both Blagojevic and Popovic as a Defence demographer, whether any of her criticisms were actually correct and could you point out the correct criticisms she made?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. After looking at the list of missing, she identified a number or a small number of duplicates and criticised us for that. We looked at this and found that she was right in some of these cases, and, indeed, we had identified these same records as duplicates when we did the analysis. But we had, through an oversight, forgotten to remove the extra duplicates, because we had to make a decision on which of two almost identical records should be removed. And we also did some further analysis, we identified a few more duplicates and removed those that were incorrect or real duplicates. But Mrs. Radovanovic, in fact, also found some false duplicates where the records looked almost -- looked identical, almost identical, as pointed out previously, but they were not, in fact, identical. This is a question of twins and brothers, et cetera, where the information are -- is almost the same but they are still representing different individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You may not know the exact numbers but can you give us just the rough numbers of where she was correct and --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think it was, like, between five and ten, something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think you've said after looking and confirming she was right in that number, you went on and found a few more that you found yourself as duplicates. Do you remember how many more roughly you found --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I would need to check that in the report. And there are additional report, our rebuttal report, but I can do that tonight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: But I would like to point out that some of the duplicates that she found were false duplicates and a few were correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is this correction reflected in the last version of your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And also in the 2005 version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any other things that she pointed out that you had to correct on your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: She mentioned that what we did, this kind of matching or record linkage was unscientific, not done before, but it has been done before, and we have -- we can refer then to a large literature on record linkage. For example, by name which is a complicated procedure and there's an annex in a report that discusses this record linkage methodology. It is Annex 5. This is discussed -- there is a large scientific literature on this. It's not something that we invented from scratch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. But my question was anything that you found justified. I know she had a long report with other criticism but any justified criticisms aside from what you have said?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And since we're on the topic of mistakes or errors, have you, in the last few days, had a chance to carefully go through your 2009 report, which is 07170, and did you identify any -- any mistakes there?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, a few. There are several minor typos of a more grammatical or typo nature but there are also some errors that could be misleading. In such a large report there are many details and when you re-read it after three years, you see new things. So, on page 22, in the report, in the English version, page 22, second -- no, third paragraph from the top --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a second. Page 22 English, that should be B/C/S page 25.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The second sentence that paragraph reads: "The remaining 29.5 per cent have not yet been identified as dead but the proportion keeps increasing." It should, of course, have been "decreasing."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Because as more people are identified, less people are not identified. So it's logical. I don't think anybody would misunderstand that. But it was just a small logical error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are referring to the paragraph above the chapter 1.5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 2.5, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, yes 2.5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you pointed out another mistake on page 26 of the English, should be page 30 of the B/C/S, and I believe it was the second big paragraph in the English, right above the paragraph 2.6 in the B/C/S. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct. It's just above the -- the section 2.6. The last five words in that -- the last sentence above should be deleted. The words "compare to their preceding cohorts." The reason is that it is not clear what the preceding cohorts or preceding ages -- whether they are preceding ages. The point is that age group 15 to 19 have very high fatality rates which can you see from Table 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So just explain what's wrong with that sentence, why you want it deleted now?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: If you interpret the preceding cohorts as age group 20 to 24, that higher risk of disappearance is lower and not higher. So -- but it generally high, but it's not higher for all places of -- for all municipalities. So that's why we just want to make it -- point out they have very high risk of disappearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any other significant mistakes you want to call our attention to?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now as I'd mentioned in the summary, there were some complaints that the ICRC list was exaggerated, and, in fact, the -- in the Tolimir trial brief on page 114 to 115, it appears that he is suggesting that the 1996 census -- sorry, the 1996 voters' registration list contained many of the names on your missing list, thereby suggesting your missing list is invalid because the people on the voters' list were alive. Can you -- have you heard of this complaint before?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah, this is a repeated criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is it a valid criticism?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Because the 1996 voters' list is -- was the 1991 census. According to the Dayton Accord of November 1995, the 1991 census should be used as a voters' list for the first election, because it was -- well, not time or it was not possible to establish proper voters' lists. So anybody who was on the 1991 census could vote in 1996. So then it is not surprising that it would include a number of persons who were listed as missing. They did not have to register actively to vote as they did in 1997 and later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that process you described of people coming in and registering, that first started in what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I made a mistake, I shouldn't have said pages in the Defence trial brief, I should have said paragraphs 114 to 115 where this allegation is made. And the other allegations, are they dealt with in your 2009 report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Some are. Some have been left. They were -- these -- the major allegations were addressed in the 2000 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I don't -- I don't think, given that they're addressed in the purpose of this testimony, that we need go into that. And, Mr. President, I would like to offer the 2009 reports now in evidence, that's 65 ter 07170, and 07171, 07173, and 4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: All these four documents will be received as exhibits and assigned exhibit numbers now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just one minor clarification. If I'm understanding it correctly, whether 65 ter document 07170A is also tendered? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In my understanding this should be part of 65 ter 07170. But, Mr. McCloskey, please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we put 07170A up on the screen. I believe this is something that Dr. Brunborg would like to replace with the 07170 -- sorry. In any event, give me one second, if you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I didn't mean to suggest he was replacing the whole report. This, as with can see, is a table.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's my understanding, Dr. Brunborg, you would prefer to replace this table with the similar table that is in the original report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. The reason is purely editorial but only the first page was printed or included in the first report. So the rest of the pages were missing by an editorial oversight or technical oversight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So there are -- in fact, this is a total of five pages, this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Should that be treated as a part of the report, 65 ter 07170?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It should replace the -- the table that is on the original report which is at page 97 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should avoid to have a different P number for that part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it is on page 104 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, is this a clear situation now for you?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I think I'm good at understanding that 65 ter 07170A is not to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be part of the report. 65 ter 07170 should be merged, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. However, you could it that. So we want it into evidence just merged as part of the report.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, now it is clear. Therefore, the following exhibit numbers shall be assigned: 07170 shall be assigned Exhibit P1776. 65 ter 07171 shall be assigned Exhibit 1777. 65 ter document 07173 shall be assigned Exhibit P1778. And 65 ter document 07174 shall be assigned Exhibit P1779. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have nothing further. We may have a -- a slight change of numbers on that last thing. Ms. Stewart will explain to me. I may have created a problem. But we'll sort that out. But as for the witness, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, your cross-examination, please. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Once again, I would like to greet everybody present in the courtroom. I would like to greet the witness, and I wish that this testimony ends in accordance with God's will and not my will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have for you the following questions: First of all, can you tell us whether, during your research, or during drafting of your article or report, you endeavoured to find out how many people were unlawfully killed and in how many cases death was caused by some unlawful acts. Specifically, have you managed to find out who died in combat and who died after combat?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Thank you. You seem to ask several questions in -- and important questions. And, first, I was not asked to distinguish or focus or lawful or unlawful killings. That was not part of my task. I'm a demographer, and not a lawyer. I don't really know what is an unlawful killing. But I know, of course, that being killed in combat is legally different from being killed in -- not in combat. And we don't -- we do not have data to distinguish between those who are killed in combat or not. The only thing we have is the number of missing but it has later, through exhumations, become clear that most of the missing persons that have been identified as dead have been found in mass graves where they also have been people are -- have been blind-folded or shot from the back at a short distance. So the indications are that -- well, this lawful, not lawful, I will not touch upon. But it seems like most of the missing persons were not killed in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... I apologise for not having switched on the microphone. Can you tell us, this majority that you mention, what percentage would that be? You just mentioned people that were killed in combat and yet found their place in your lists. So what percentage are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I do not have a percentage. I did not say how many people are killed in combat. I don't know even if any were killed in combat. But I know that as people started walking through the forests towards Tuzla there may have been some combats. There may be not. I know there was shooting at the column of people who waled through the forests, but nobody, as far as I know, has been able to determine how many died in combat during that march. Some additional figures. We have analysed and looked at the number of soldiers, those who were registered with the Bosnian army, in the list of missing, and we found that 70 per cent of the missing were also listed in the army archives as being dead or missing. But the army lists do not include place of death or circumstances of death, so they cannot be used to -- to tell us anything about whether they died in combat or not. Moreover, in the list, in the army list, there are also civilians -- well, not active soldiers. So, again, it is not possible to tell from the army documents whether people army -- registered in the army were killed in combat or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
